The MOC Products Limited Warranty is a vehicle protection program backed by MOC Products Company, Inc.

TO QUALIFY: Vehicle must be (1) less than 100,000 miles on the odometer, (2) less than 10 years old as of January 1st of the model year, (3) maintained per the manufacturer's recommended schedule, (4) gross vehicle weight 12,500 lbs or less, (5) privately-owned passenger car, van, SUV, or pickup used exclusively for personal use.
TO MAINTAIN BENEFITS: Engine service every 10,000 miles.
WAITING PERIOD: Vehicle protection becomes effective only after 60 days OR 750 miles (1,200 km), whichever occurs LAST.
COVERAGE LIMITS: Up to $4,000 protection per covered system.
REPAIR PROCEDURE: If a covered failure occurs, the customer or shop must contact MOC Warranty Department at 800-928-9880 BEFORE any repair work begins.
WHAT'S COVERED: Repair or replacement of specifically-listed lubricated parts within each covered system that fail due to abnormal wear or corrosion.

WHAT'S NOT COVERED (Universal Exclusions): Commercial use (taxi, fleet, delivery, rental, police, off-road, racing, snow removal, construction); vehicles for towing without factory tow package; vehicles with rebuilt or salvage titles; gray-market vehicles; vehicles with altered or non-functioning odometers; pre-existing conditions; collision/fire/theft/vandalism/flood/lightning/earthquake/hail/windstorm/freezing damage; manufacturer recall components; non-MOC fluid use; failure to maintain proper fluid levels; DIY service of any kind.

Direct-injection (DI) engines have a fundamental decarb limitation: chemical decarb services CAN'T effectively reach the back side of intake valves on direct-only engines, because the fuel (which carries the cleaner in port-injected engines) never touches the valves. For DI engines with documented carbon buildup symptoms (misfires, rough idle, power loss), the actual fix is mechanical — walnut blasting at the dealer, $400-$700 typical cost. Chemical decarb on a DI engine is preventive maintenance, not remediation.

Iridium tip technology is the modern standard — and the difference between iridium and platinum isn't a marketing tier, it's a real engineering advantage. Iridium melts at 4,470°F (vs 3,225°F for platinum), enabling a 0.4-0.6mm center electrode (vs 1.1mm for platinum). The smaller tip concentrates the spark, improves cold-start ignition, and extends service life to 100,000+ miles.
